The Fifth Amendment. To the United States Constitution, ratified in seventeen ninety-one as part of the Bill of Rights. It protects individuals against self-incrimination and the deprivation of life, liberty, or property without due process of law. It grants grand jury protections, double jeopardy prohibitions, and eminent domain limits. The Fifth Amendment stands as one of the most powerful shields against state power in American law.

The Self-Incrimination Clause reads: No person shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself. This is the amendment's most recognizable provision, invoked when witnesses take the Fifth. The Due Process Clause states: nor be deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law. It has spawned centuries of constitutional litigation over the scope of fundamental rights. The Double Jeopardy prohibition prevents prosecution twice for the same offense, ensuring finality in criminal adjudication. The Grand Jury requirement in federal felony cases mandates that serious charges be reviewed by citizens before prosecution proceeds. The Takings Clause declares: nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation. It limits eminent domain and has evolved to address environmental and zoning disputes. Miranda v. Arizona in nineteen sixty-six operationalized the Fifth Amendment's protections by requiring police to inform suspects of their right to remain silent and have counsel. The amendment has been selectively incorporated into the Fourteenth Amendment, applying most, though not all, of its protections to the states. The Fifth Amendment connects to the United States Constitution as the document it amends as part of the Bill of Rights; the Bill of Rights as the first ten amendments, of which the Fifth is a central protection of individual liberty; due process as a constitutional guarantee the Fifth Amendment enshrines, spawning ongoing litigation; Miranda v. Arizona as the Supreme Court case that operationalized Fifth Amendment protections in police interrogation; self-incrimination as the specific right the Fifth Amendment most famously protects; and the Fourteenth Amendment which selectively incorporated Fifth Amendment protections, applying them to state action.
